title: Stages of Child Development: Three to Six Years and Six to Eight Years
summary: Preschoolers develop muscle coordination and abilities to think and speak; observation, memory and verbal skills improve; they learn self-help skills like dressing and feeding and learn to separate from family.

Physical-motor: growth is slower than in infancy but steady — about 4–5 pounds and 2–3 inches a year; they need less sleep. Gross motor: better at running, jumping, throwing and kicking; catch a bounced ball; pedal a tricycle at about three and steer at four; hop on one foot at about four; heel-to-toe walk at about five. Fine motor: draw a circle, square and triangle; use blunt scissors; dress with supervision; manage a spoon and fork; spread with a knife; button clothes and tie shoelaces.

Socio-emotional: self-concept based on concrete, observable features (name, possessions, family, 'I run fast'); gender identity forms and children prefer gender-typed clothes and play; social skills for playing with others; four-to-five-year-olds play games with rules that keep changing. They can talk about their feelings; complex emotions such as guilt, shame and pride emerge. Erikson: children want to take initiative; if always stopped, they develop guilt.

Cognitive (Piaget's pre-operational stage, 2–7): symbolic function (thinking of objects not present, naming with words and numbers); spatial thinking (a picture can stand for something real); causality (thinking about causes but linking events that happen close together); categorisation (similarities and differences) and identities; animism (life-like qualities given to non-living things); lack of conservation (a longer row of coins seems to have more); egocentrism, shown by Piaget's three-mountain task.

Language: vocabulary expands; fast mapping — quickly grasping the meaning of a new word from context; plurals, possessives and past tense from three; pragmatics — the practical, social use of language. Competencies: pronouns and prepositions, three-word sentences, size words, three-step commands, counting to ten, naming four colours, enjoying rhymes, answering 'why' questions, talking to oneself.
## Six to eight years (early primary stage)

Physical: growth of 1–3 inches a year, faster weight gain at eight to nine, large muscles more developed than small ones, 'baby fat' decreases, muscle tone and body control improve. Socio-emotional: a more complete, realistic self-concept based on both outer and inner traits ('I am good'); can verbalise conflicting and complex emotions; wants privacy and emotional freedom; peer groups, competitive games and teamwork; developing sense of right and wrong.

Cognitive: more logical but still concrete thinking; can remember routes to familiar places; conserves number, length, liquid, weight, area and volume; reversible thought; no longer egocentric; longer and selective attention; plans ahead; reads and writes. Language: humour, turn-taking and sustained conversation; better vocabulary and syntax; social use of words with different people; invents new words and phrases.

Froebel: play is a serious occupation for the child; Montessori stressed free, spontaneous play; Piaget: play is responses repeated for functional pleasure; Freud: the child at play behaves like a creative writer. Play lays the foundation for literacy, is learning, gives choice, lets children practise movement and test limits, lets adults read children's body language, and is fun. It supports physical-motor development (fine and gross skills, stamina), socio-emotional development (self-esteem, coping with feelings, negotiating roles and rules), cognitive development (counting, colours, problem solving), language development (rules of language, words, jokes, riddles) and art and aesthetic appreciation.

vsa: How does the growth rate of children aged three to six years compare with that of infants?
Three-to-six-year-olds grow more slowly than infants but steadily — about 4–5 pounds and 2–3 inches a year — and need less sleep; their muscles and bones grow stronger and coordination improves.

vsa: What is a key aspect of preschoolers' socio-emotional development?

A growing self-concept: preschoolers describe themselves by concrete features — name, possessions, family, achievements ('I run fast'). They can talk about their feelings, complex emotions such as guilt, shame and pride appear, they learn social skills for playing with others, and they want to take initiative.
April 2025
What emerges during preschool age regarding gender identity?
Children classify themselves as male or female, prefer clothes and dressing suited to their own gender, use gender-typed language, and their play tends to reflect gendered practices.
April 2025
What is causality in preschool children's thinking?

The ability to think about the causes of familiar events, such as living things growing when they get food. But preschoolers cannot yet reason logically about cause and effect and may link two events that happen close together as cause and effect.

vsa: What is symbolic function?
The preschooler's ability to keep an image of an object, person or event in mind and think about it without it being present, and to name it with symbols such as words and numbers.

vsa: What is spatial thinking in preschoolers?

Understanding spatial relationships — for example, that a picture represents something not present but real — though preschoolers may not fully understand the relation between the picture and the actual object.

sa: Explain the different aspects of cognitive development of preschoolers.

Preschoolers are in Piaget's pre-operational stage. Symbolic function: they think of absent objects and use words and numbers as symbols. Spatial thinking: they understand that a picture stands for a real object. Causality: they think about causes of familiar events but may link events just because they happen together. Categorisation: they group objects as edible/inedible, friend/non-friend, but also show animism. Identities: they partly understand that objects stay the same when their form changes, but lack conservation. Egocentrism: they see only their own viewpoint (three-mountain task).
List the abilities of a seven-year-old child in the cognitive, language and socio-emotional domains.

Cognitive: logical but concrete thinking, conservation of number, length, liquid and weight, reversibility, remembering routes, planning ahead, longer and selective attention, reading and writing. Language: sophisticated comprehension and use, clear speech to share opinions, turn-taking and sustained conversation, appreciation of humour, inventing words. Socio-emotional: realistic self-concept from strengths and weaknesses, verbalising conflicting emotions, wanting privacy, competitive games and teamwork with peers, developing sense of right and wrong.
Describe the language development of preschool children.

Vocabulary expands rapidly and they use words easily in everyday talk; fast mapping helps them learn new words from context. They combine words into sentences and from three use plurals, possessives and past tense, and pronouns like I, me, you, we correctly. They become competent in pragmatics — knowing how to speak with whom, repeating or rephrasing when not understood. They can follow three-step commands, count to ten, name four colours, enjoy rhymes, answer 'why' questions and talk to themselves.
la: What do you understand by play? Discuss the role of play in early childhood development.

Play is a child's freely chosen, joyful activity; Froebel called it a serious occupation, Montessori stressed free and spontaneous play, and Piaget defined it as responses repeated for functional pleasure. Role: it lays the foundation for literacy (new sounds and words), is itself learning, gives choice and lets children test their physical limits, and lets adults understand children's body language. Physical-motor: hopping, skipping and using writing tools build gross and fine skills, stamina and confidence. Socio-emotional: children control their play world, which builds self-esteem; they learn to cope with feelings, cooperate, negotiate roles and follow rules. Cognitive: counting, colours and problem solving. Language: internalising language rules and using language for different purposes, jokes and riddles. Aesthetic: creating and appreciating art.
Make a comparative milestone chart of a three-year-old and a six-year-old child.

Physical-motor — three: runs, jumps, pedals a tricycle, scribbles, draws a circle, feeds self with a spoon; six: hops and balances on one foot, heel-to-toe walk, steers well, cuts a straight line with scissors, draws a triangle, dresses self, ties shoelaces. Socio-emotional — three: self-awareness, gender identity forming, plays beside or with a few peers, names basic feelings; six: describes self by abilities, plays cooperative games with rules, talks about feelings, shows guilt, shame and pride, takes initiative. Cognitive — three: symbolic thought, animism, egocentrism, no conservation; six: categorises, thinks about causes, beginning to overcome egocentrism, still pre-operational. Language — three: three-word sentences, plurals and past tense begin; six: long sentences, pragmatics, follows three-step commands, counts to ten, names colours, enjoys word play.
